client: I've been struggling a lot lately since my partner moved abroad for work about six months ago. The distance has made me feel really lonely, like I'm going through my daily life in this kind of fog, and our relationship feels more and more disconnected even though we still talk. Honestly, I wasn't sure about coming here because I don't know if talking about it is really going to change the fact that they're just... not here.
therapist: What you're carrying sounds really heavy — six months of missing someone who's still *in* your life but feels so far away, and that foggy, disconnected feeling makes a lot of sense given what you're navigating. I also notice there's something tender in how you're speaking about this, like part of you is holding back, maybe even doubting whether you deserve to take up space with this pain. It's okay that you're uncertain about being here — that doubt doesn't have to go away before we can start, and while talking won't bring your partner home, it might help you feel a little less alone in that fog.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I appreciate you saying that, but I'm not sure I'm holding back so much as I just... don't really see the point in dwelling on it when nothing's going to change. And honestly, the "deserving to take up space" thing feels a bit off to me, because it's not that I think my pain doesn't matter, it's more that I feel guilty even being sad when my partner is the one who had to uproot their whole life for this job. Like, they're the one dealing with the hard stuff, and I'm just sitting here feeling sorry for myself.
therapist: Thank you for correcting me — that's really helpful, and it makes a lot of sense that guilt is at the center of this rather than feeling undeserving. I notice you're speaking quite quickly, like there's a lot of pressure behind these words, which makes me wonder if part of you has been working hard to talk yourself out of your own pain for a while now. But here's something worth gently examining: your partner uprooting their life and you struggling with loneliness aren't in competition — both things can be hard at the same time, and your sadness doesn't take anything away from what they're going through.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and logically I know it's not a competition, but it doesn't really feel that way when we're on a call and they're exhausted from a hard day and I don't want to pile my stuff on top of that. So I end up just... not saying anything, and then I feel even more alone after we hang up. It's like the guilt is actually making the disconnection worse, but I don't know how to talk to them without feeling like a burden.
therapist: You've actually just identified something really important — the guilt isn't just a feeling you're carrying privately, it's actively shaping your behavior in a way that creates the very disconnection you're trying to avoid, which is a painful cycle to be caught in. I can hear in your voice a kind of urgency, like you've been turning this over and over and it feels almost unsolvable. But it's worth gently questioning that "burden" thought — is it based on evidence that your partner doesn't want to hear from you, or is it an assumption that's quietly making the decision for both of you?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean, they've never actually said they don't want to hear about my feelings, so I guess it is more of an assumption. But they do get visibly tired on our calls, and sometimes they cut things short because of the time difference, so it doesn't feel like a completely made-up fear either. I think part of me is scared that if I actually test that assumption and open up, and they do seem overwhelmed or distant, that'll hurt even more than just staying quiet.
therapist: What you just said takes real honesty — you're not dismissing the fear, you're naming it precisely: that opening up and being met with distance would feel like confirmation of something you're dreading, and staying quiet at least keeps that possibility at bay. I can hear how much tension is sitting behind that thought, like you're bracing for something even as you're talking about it. But it's worth sitting with this — right now, without testing it, you're already experiencing the painful outcome you're trying to avoid, so the silence isn't actually protecting you from disconnection, it's just making it quieter.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That actually lands in a way I wasn't expecting, because you're right that I'm already feeling disconnected, so in some ways I have nothing to lose by trying. But the thing is, even if the logic makes sense, I don't really know how to just suddenly start opening up when we've fallen into this pattern of keeping things surface-level for months now. It feels like trying to change the rules of something mid-game without the other person even knowing the rules were a problem.
therapist: That metaphor you used — changing the rules mid-game — is really vivid, and it tells me you're not resistant to opening up, you're genuinely uncertain about *how*, which is a much more workable place to be. There's something soft and careful in the way you're speaking about this, like you're handling it delicately, and I wonder if that same gentleness could actually be the way in — not a sudden dramatic opening up, but something small, like telling your partner "I've been missing you more than I've been letting on lately." Sometimes the door back to each other doesn't need to be thrown open all at once.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That's a much smaller step than what I was imagining, and I think that's why it feels slightly less terrifying. But I'm still worried about the timing, like, what if I say that and they're distracted or tired and just kind of brush past it, because then I'd feel even more invisible than I do now. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to set up the conversation so it doesn't just get swallowed by the usual small talk and time pressure.
therapist: The way you're speaking — softly but quickly, like you're thinking it through even as you say it — tells me this feels both hopeful and fragile at the same time, and that fear of being brushed past is really understandable given how invisible you've already been feeling. You're actually asking a really practical and self-aware question though, and the answer might be as simple as asking for the conversation before having it — something like telling your partner "I'd love to have a call soon where we're not rushed, there's something I've been wanting to share with you." That way you're not ambushing a tired moment, you're creating a space together, which also sends a signal that what you have to say matters.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That actually feels like something I could realistically do, and I like that it gives my partner a heads-up rather than just dropping something heavy on them out of nowhere. I think my worry now is more about what happens on my end, like, even if I set up the conversation perfectly, I'm not sure I'll actually be able to say what I need to say when the moment comes because I've been bottling this up for so long that I don't even know how to put it into words anymore. It's like I've gotten so used to suppressing it that I'm not sure I can just access it on demand.
therapist: What you're describing — that feeling of reaching inward for something and not quite finding it — makes complete sense after months of carefully packing it away, and I notice there's something almost anxious in how you're speaking about it, like you're worried you've lost access to yourself. But here's something worth considering: you've actually been finding the words this whole conversation, describing the fog, the guilt, the fear of being brushed past — that *is* the bottled-up feeling, already surfacing. What if the preparation for that conversation with your partner looked a little like what we've been doing here — just letting yourself speak without it needing to be perfect?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hadn't really thought about it that way, that what I've been doing here is actually the same thing I'm afraid I can't do with my partner. But talking to you feels different because there's no stakes, like you're not going to get tired or check the time or make me feel like I'm too much, whereas with my partner all of that is possible and that changes everything about how safe it feels to just... let it out. I guess I'm not sure how to recreate that kind of low-pressure feeling when the person on the other end is the one I'm most afraid of disappointing.
therapist: What you just named is really important — the safety here comes from the absence of stakes, and with your partner the stakes are everything, which makes vulnerability feel so much more exposing. I notice your voice is soft but moving quickly, like there's something tender and a little raw sitting just beneath the surface of these words. It might help to remember that the goal of that conversation isn't to perform vulnerability perfectly, but to let your partner *in* — and part of creating that safety can actually come from naming the fear itself, something like "I want to tell you something but I'm scared of feeling like too much," because that honesty about the fear can lower the stakes before you've even said the harder thing.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Naming the fear out loud to my partner before even getting to the main thing, that's something I hadn't considered and it actually feels more honest than trying to just launch into it. But I think part of me worries that saying "I'm scared of feeling like too much" might itself come across as too much, like I'm already making the conversation about my anxiety before I've even said what I need to say. I don't know, maybe I'm overthinking it, but it feels like there's no clean way in that doesn't risk something.
therapist: There's something in the way you're speaking — softly but quickly, at a pitch that carries a kind of quiet tension — that tells me you're working really hard right now to find the "right" way in, almost like you're trying to solve your way out of vulnerability. But I want to gently reflect something back: you just said "maybe I'm overthinking it," and I think part of you already knows that the search for a clean, riskless entry point is itself a way of staying safe. There may not be a perfect door in — but "there's something I've been wanting to say and I'm not sure how to start" is honest, it's human, and it's already an invitation.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Yeah, I think you're right that I've been trying to engineer my way around the scary part instead of just... going through it. That phrase you suggested, "there's something I've been wanting to say and I'm not sure how to start," feels almost too simple, but maybe that's actually why it could work, because it's not dressed up or rehearsed. I'm still scared, but I think I've been waiting for the fear to go away before I do anything, and maybe that's just not how it works.
therapist: What you just said is genuinely one of the hardest things to accept — that the fear doesn't have to be gone before you can move, that courage isn't the absence of fear but doing it while the fear is still there. I can hear something in your voice that sounds like you're right at the edge of something, a little breathless, like this is landing in a real way rather than just an intellectual one. You've spent this whole conversation finding your way toward that truth, and I think some part of you already knew it — you just needed space to let yourself arrive at it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech
